Board-Ready Indicators · November 2026

Te Kōtuku ki te Rangi

KPI Dashboard

Your Board explored these five KPIs together at the June 2026 workshop. Together they show whether the organisation is financially healthy, building partnerships that deliver, and hearing from whaiora.

Each KPI has its own page. Together, its sections form the KPI Record that the KPI Policy asks for: what the KPI measures, how it is reported, the reasoning behind it, and its Decision History. Open a KPI to see what it is asking to be achieved, what your Board still needs to decide, and the decisions made about it so far.

This dashboard uses the Board's records up to July 2026.

KPI 1A | Grow Revenue

“Grow revenue by 10% in the year to 30 June 2026.”

IWhat this KPI meansWhat the KPI is asking to be achieved, and why your Board has set it▾
It means
Total revenue for the year is at least 10% higher than in the baseline year. The audited financial statements confirm the result.
It does not mean
Growth of any kind. One-off contract income can meet the 10% and still leave the organisation no better funded the next year. That is why one-off income is identified separately, in the baseline and in the Evidence Map.
Why your Board set it
KPI 1A and KPI 1B are a pair: KPI 1A tracks revenue and KPI 1B tracks the margin. Together they show how the Board is looking after the organisation's financial resources. Every service the organisation runs depends on its revenue.
Target difficulty
The 2025–27 contract envelope is about $1.37 million, and it stays broadly flat from year to year. So most of the 10% would need to come from new revenue, which is what the pipeline of funding bids tracks.
What it protects against
Finding out about a funding shortfall only when the audit arrives. It also protects against a growth story that rests on forecasts alone.
Link to the strategy
Financial sustainability. The Strategic Plan's priority targets can be added here once the Board confirms them.

IIIEarly-warning indicators and action thresholdsHow your Board would get early warning if this KPI is going off track▾

A revenue target only protects the Board if the Board can see a possible shortfall while there is still time to act. Early-warning indicators improve the Board's view. They cannot guarantee the result.

Leading indicator (early warning)
The forecast of funding bids (RFPs) and their total value. The Board chose this at the June 2026 workshop. If the pipeline of bids shrinks, the Board gets an early sign of a possible shortfall, well before the audited result.
Supporting measures
The CEO's reports would show three numbers side by side: (i) the total value of live bids, (ii) how many bids become contracts, and (iii) revenue compared with the same period last year. A forecast on its own can mislead, because a bid only becomes revenue once it is won.
Lagging indicator (final result)
Total annual revenue, confirmed through the audited financial statements once the year is over. The outcome measure is annual revenue growth. The audited statements are the evidence source.

Proposed action thresholds, for your Board to confirm

An action threshold does not always need a full Board decision. Some start a management investigation, with the result reported to the Board afterwards.

Too few bids in the pipeline

When action is triggered
At the end of any quarter, the value of live bids is less than three times the revenue still needed to reach 10%.
Agreed response
Management: The CEO reviews the pipeline and plans further bids.
Board escalation: The CEO reports the gap and the plan to the Audit, Finance and Risk Committee, which reports to the next Board hui.
Why this point
Not every bid is won. Three times the gap assumes that about one bid in three succeeds, a common planning rule. Once the Board knows how many of its own bids become contracts (a supporting measure above), it can adjust the multiple.

Bids are not becoming contracts

When action is triggered
Two quarters in a row pass with no bid won and no other new revenue.
Agreed response
Management: The CEO prepares a revised revenue plan, e.g. more bids, different funders or other income.
Board escalation: The revised plan goes to the Audit, Finance and Risk Committee, and the Board hears it at its next hui.
Why this point
One quarter without a win can be normal timing. Two in a row suggests a pattern.

Revenue is behind at the half-year

When action is triggered
Revenue is tracking below about 5% growth at the half-year, and no seasonal catch-up has been minuted.
Agreed response
Management: The CEO explains the causes and proposes actions.
Board escalation: The Board agrees an action to address the shortfall, and minutes it.
Why this point
5% is half of the year's target. Below that, the second half of the year would need to do better than the first, so the Board needs to judge early whether that is realistic.

VIChanging this KPIHow the Change Protocol in the KPI Policy applies to this KPI▾

This KPI follows the Change Protocol in the KPI Policy. Major changes require Board approval, while changes to monitoring may be approved under the CEO's delegated authority. The notes below are specific to KPI 1A.

  • Who may propose a change. The CEO, the Board, or a Board Committee (the Personnel Committee or the Audit, Finance and Risk Committee).
  • Proposing a major change. Any proposed major change must be put to the Board in writing, explaining:
    • What specifically is proposed to change?
    • Why is the change necessary?
    • How will it affect the target, measurement, or comparison with previous results?
    • Who has been consulted, and what decision is requested?
  • Who approves. The Board approves major changes, ordinarily on a recommendation from the Audit, Finance and Risk Committee. Because this is a financial KPI, the Audit, Finance and Risk Committee is the natural recommender. Changes to leading indicators or action thresholds may be approved by the CEO where authorised, unless they are significant.
  • Where it is recorded. Minuted at the meeting, with the change proposal linked as reference material, and a new entry added to the KPI Record's Decision History.
  • What to expect. Leading indicators and action thresholds may be refined over time as the Board and management learn which measures provide the most useful early warning. Changes are approved according to the Change Protocol.
  • Open change request. The CEO's rolling-target proposal of 11 November 2025. Under the Change Protocol it needs a written proposal and a Board decision. The outcome belongs in the KPI Record's Decision History either way. See Matters for future review in Section II.

IWhat this KPI meansWhat the KPI is asking to be achieved, and why your Board has set it▾
It means
The net profit margin stays at or above 5% all the way to 30 June 2026. The audited financial statements confirm the result.
It does not mean
A 5% margin reached by putting off needed spending or reducing service quality. A short note on any spending put off would guard against this (see Section II).
Why your Board set it
KPI 1B is the second half of the financial pair with KPI 1A. Revenue can grow while costs grow faster. The margin shows whether the organisation is living within its means.
Target difficulty
A 16.11% margin was reported in November 2025, so 5% looks reachable on current figures. The minutes questioned whether that level is sustainable, which is why the note on spending put off matters.
What it protects against
Finding out about a squeeze on the margin only at the end of the year. It also protects against a year that looks profitable only because spending was put off.

IIIEarly-warning indicators and action thresholdsHow your Board would get early warning if this KPI is going off track▾

A problem with the margin can build for months without anyone noticing. Costs rise a little, income drops a little, and the Board often hears about it first in the audit. Early-warning indicators improve the Board's view. They cannot guarantee the result.

Leading indicator (early warning)
None chosen yet. The bids forecast used for KPI 1A shows where revenue is heading, but not where costs are heading. Two options would give early warning on the margin: the monthly management accounts, or the cost-to-income ratio (the share of income spent on costs) compared with budget.
Lagging indicator (final result)
The net profit margin, confirmed through the audited financial statements once the year is over. The outcome measure is the margin. The audited statements are the evidence source.

Proposed action thresholds, for your Board to confirm

An action threshold does not always need a full Board decision. Some start a management investigation, with the result reported to the Board afterwards.

Margin below 5%

When action is triggered
The monthly management accounts show a net margin below 5% for two months in a row.
Agreed response
Management: The CEO investigates the causes.
Board escalation: The CEO brings a plan for costs and income to the Audit, Finance and Risk Committee, which reports to the Board.
Why this point
One month can dip because of when payments fall. Two months in a row is more likely a trend.

Costs running ahead of budget

When action is triggered
At the end of any quarter, the cost-to-income ratio is above budget.
Agreed response
Management: The CEO reviews spending against budget and reports the causes to the Audit, Finance and Risk Committee.
Board escalation: If costs are not expected to come back to budget, the Audit, Finance and Risk Committee reports to the next Board hui.
Why this point
The budget is the plan the Board agreed for the year. A quarter above it is early enough to act before the year-end margin is set.

Margin held by putting off spending

When action is triggered
The 5% is met while planned investment, maintenance or service quality is put off.
Agreed response
Management: The CEO reports the spending put off as a one-line note beside the margin.
Board escalation: The Board considers whether the margin is sustainable, and minutes any response.
Why this point
A margin reached by delaying spending moves the cost into a later year. This is the risk named at gate 3.

KPI 6A | Establish Strategic Partnerships

Governance KPIMaihi | Performance
KPI 6A wording

“Establish two new strategic partnerships by Sep 2026, each delivering at least one joint initiative, project or service.”

How it is measured: partnerships that lead to shared work, recorded in an updated Partnership Register.

IWhat this KPI meansWhat the KPI is asking to be achieved, and why your Board has set it▾
It means
By September 2026, there are two new strategic partnerships, and each one is already delivering a joint initiative, project or service.
Who counts
Any organisation that the Board confirms as a strategic partner. An MOU is not required.
It does not mean
Counting signed MOUs. A partnership counts only once it delivers something together with the organisation.
Why your Board set it
Partnerships bring the organisation reach, shared delivery and funding. KPI 6A tracks whether new partnerships are being formed. KPI 6B tracks whether partnerships keep working, and KPI 6C tracks whether whaiora are better off.
What it protects against
Signed agreements that do not lead to any shared work.

IIIEarly-warning indicators and action thresholdsHow your Board would get early warning if this KPI is going off track▾

These indicators show whether each partnership is moving towards shared work. They improve the Board's view of progress. They cannot guarantee the result.

Leading indicators (early warning)
MOU status, recent meetings, how regularly catch-ups happen, and joint programmes being planned. If catch-ups become less frequent, or no joint work is planned, the Board gets an early sign that a partnership may be stalling.
Where they will be recorded
The Partnership Register would hold all of this. It has not been set up yet, so the Board cannot see these indicators yet.
Lagging indicator (final result)
The number of new partnerships that have delivered a joint initiative, project or service, shown in the Partnership Register.

Proposed action thresholds, for your Board to confirm

An action threshold does not always need a full Board decision. Some start a management investigation, with the result reported to the Board afterwards.

No Partnership Register

When action is triggered
The register is not set up at least one month before the KPI's target date.
Agreed response
Management: The CEO sets a date to set it up, and names who keeps it.
Board escalation: If no date is set, the Board makes setting up the register a minuted action, with a named owner and date.
Why this point
Without the register the Board cannot see the indicators or verify the result. A month leaves time to record each partnership before the result is judged.

Partnerships not moving

When action is triggered
Two months before the target date, fewer than two partnerships are planning joint work.
Agreed response
Management: The CEO reviews the prospects and reports the options.
Board escalation: The Board discusses with the CEO whether the target is still reachable, and minutes the response.
Why this point
Joint work takes time to plan. Two months out is about the last point at which a new joint project could still start in time.

A partnership with no shared work

When action is triggered
A partnership has been signed, but a quarter later no joint initiative, project or service is planned.
Agreed response
Management: The CEO agrees next steps with the partner.
Board escalation: The CEO's next Board report says what the partnership will deliver and by when, or why it should not count.
Why this point
The KPI counts a partnership only once it delivers shared work. A quarter is long enough for a first joint plan to appear.

VIChanging this KPIHow the Change Protocol in the KPI Policy applies to this KPI▾

This KPI follows the Change Protocol in the KPI Policy. Major changes require Board approval, while changes to monitoring may be approved under the CEO's delegated authority. The notes below are specific to KPI 6A.

  • Who may propose a change. The CEO, the Board, or a Board Committee (the Personnel Committee or the Audit, Finance and Risk Committee).
  • Proposing a major change. Any proposed major change must be put to the Board in writing, explaining:
    • What specifically is proposed to change?
    • Why is the change necessary?
    • How will it affect the target, measurement, or comparison with previous results?
    • Who has been consulted, and what decision is requested?
  • Who approves. The Board approves major changes, ordinarily on a recommendation from the Personnel Committee. The Personnel Committee would usually recommend changes, because this KPI is part of the CEO's performance framework. Changes to leading indicators or action thresholds may be approved by the CEO where authorised, unless they are significant.
  • Where it is recorded. Minuted at the meeting, with the change proposal linked as reference material, and a new entry added to the KPI Record's Decision History.
  • What to expect. Leading indicators and action thresholds may be refined over time as the Board and management learn which measures provide the most useful early warning. Changes are approved according to the Change Protocol.
  • Already required, not a change. Setting up the Partnership Register is already required by this KPI. It needs an owner and a date. It does not need a change proposal.

KPI 6B | Partnership Effectiveness

Governance KPIMaihi | Performance
KPI 6B wording

“At least 80% of strategic partnerships are rated as ‘effective’ or ‘highly effective’ in the annual external partnership review (stakeholder survey ≥7.5/10).”

What “effective” means: referrals made, joint initiatives delivered, funding gained together, improved outcomes, support plans progressed, and regular catch-ups. It covers all strategic partners, including those without an MOU.

IWhat this KPI meansWhat the KPI is asking to be achieved, and why your Board has set it▾
It means
At least 8 in 10 of the organisation's strategic partnerships are rated effective or highly effective. The partners give the rating themselves, in an independent survey, against the six measures above. A partnership needs a score of 7.5 or more out of 10.
It does not mean
Counting signed MOUs (that is KPI 6A). It also does not measure how whaiora are doing (that is KPI 6C).
Why your Board set it
A partnership that exists but does not deliver costs the organisation time and money. This KPI checks that the partnerships are helping the organisation deliver its strategy.
What it protects against
Partnerships that look fine on paper but do not lead to referrals, shared work or funding. Because an independent provider runs the survey, the people whose work is being rated are not the ones doing the rating.

IIIEarly-warning indicators and action thresholdsHow your Board would get early warning if this KPI is going off track▾

The partner survey happens once a year. Without earlier signs, the Board's first warning of a struggling partnership would be the low rating itself, a year too late to help. Early-warning indicators improve the Board's view. They cannot guarantee the result.

Leading indicators (early warning)
How regularly catch-ups happen, joint initiatives delivered, and referrals made. If these slow down, the Board gets an early sign that a rating might slip before the annual survey.
Supporting measures
The Board would look at the work and its effect together. Catch-ups can be frequent while a partner still rates the relationship poorly. Either sign on its own can mislead.
Lagging indicators (final result)
The annual effectiveness rating (the share of partnerships rated effective or highly effective) and the survey score. The outcome measure is the share rated effective. The independent survey is the evidence source.

Proposed action thresholds, for your Board to confirm

An action threshold does not always need a full Board decision. Some start a management investigation, with the result reported to the Board afterwards.

No survey provider

When action is triggered
No independent provider has been appointed five months before the survey is due.
Agreed response
Management: The CEO starts the appointment and reports the timeline.
Board escalation: The Board makes appointing the provider a minuted action, with a named owner and date.
Why this point
Five months allows time to appoint a provider, agree the rating method and run the survey before the results are due.

A partner goes quiet

When action is triggered
A strategic partner has had no catch-up for a full quarter.
Agreed response
Management: The CEO contacts the partner and decides the next step.
Board escalation: The CEO's next Board report says whether the relationship is paused, ended or needs attention, and what happens next.
Why this point
Regular catch-ups are one of the six measures of an effective partnership. A full quarter without one is a sign the relationship may be drifting.

Early signs of a low rating

When action is triggered
A mid-year check-in or direct feedback suggests a partner would score below 7.5.
Agreed response
Management: The CEO works with the partner on the issues raised.
Board escalation: The CEO brings a plan for that partnership to the Board before the annual survey.
Why this point
7.5 is the KPI's own threshold for an effective partnership.
IVKPI Definition & ReportingWhat is measured, who is accountable, and how it is reported▾
Primary measureThe share of strategic partnerships rated effective or highly effective (a score of 7.5 or more out of 10) in the annual external partnership review.
TargetAt least 80%.
TimeframeTo decideEach year. The wording says “annual” but gives no date. Proposed: the review runs and reports by the end of February, so the results are ready for the CEO's performance review in March, the timing the Personnel Committee discussed in November 2025.
BaselineNone yet, because the survey has never been run. Sector benchmarks exist, and an independent provider would bring comparisons that could set a benchmark from the first year.
KPI ownerTo decideThe CEO, named at the June 2026 workshop. Who decides which organisations count as strategic partners is still open (see Section II).
Data sourceTo decideThe independent survey provider's report, for the final result (provider not yet appointed). The Partnership Register, for progress during the year.
Reporting scheduleThe wording implies a yearly check, with nothing in between. Proposed: the Partnership Register (partner, last catch-up, initiatives and referrals) reported to the Board each quarter, and the survey results each year.
Review dateNot set yet. Proposed: the Board reviews the 80% and 7.5 thresholds after the first survey, and the wording each year after that.
Change protocolTo decideNot yet agreed. Proposed: the Change Protocol in the KPI Policy, with the Personnel Committee recommending changes. See Section VI.
Outstanding mattersTo decideThe survey provider, how the six measures combine into an “effective” rating, who confirms the partner list, the survey timing and the three action thresholds (see Section II). Until the rating method is agreed, results could not be compared fairly from one year to the next.
Things to noteReferral numbers already go to the funder each quarter, so some of the progress information already exists.

IWhat this KPI meansWhat the KPI is asking to be achieved, and why your Board has set it▾
It means
An annual survey of tāngata whaiora is completed, with at least half of tāngata whaiora taking part. Whaiora give the scores themselves.
It does not mean
That whaiora are better off, yet. As worded, the KPI measures taking part. It becomes a measure of outcomes once the Board sets targets for satisfaction and the Net Promoter Score (see Section II).
Why your Board set it
It is the only KPI that hears from whaiora directly. It asks whether tāngata whai i te ora are better off, where the other KPIs ask whether the organisation is well run.
What the results will feed
The results will shape the Board's future strategic decisions and how services are delivered.
What it protects against
Every Governance KPI showing green while the people the organisation serves are no better off.

IIIEarly-warning indicators and action thresholdsHow your Board would get early warning if this KPI is going off track▾

This section is about making sure the survey happens, reaches enough whaiora, and gives the Board results it can act on. Early-warning indicators improve the Board's view. They cannot guarantee the result.

Leading indicators (early warning)
None chosen yet. Two options would give early warning: the response rate, tracked each month while the survey is open, and signs from day-to-day service.
Lagging indicators (final result)
The completed survey. It shows the share of whaiora who took part, compared with the 50% target, and the results for satisfaction, the Net Promoter Score and the other areas. The outcome measure is participation. The provider's report is the evidence source.

Proposed action thresholds, for your Board to confirm

An action threshold does not always need a full Board decision. Some start a management investigation, with the result reported to the Board afterwards.

No provider

When action is triggered
An independent provider has not been appointed two months before the survey is due.
Agreed response
Management: The CEO completes the appointment and reports the timeline.
Board escalation: The Board makes appointing the provider a minuted action, with a named owner and date.
Why this point
A provider needs time to set up the questions and reach whaiora before the survey opens.

Questions not agreed

When action is triggered
The survey questions are not confirmed six weeks before the survey is due.
Agreed response
Management: The CEO finalises the draft questions with the provider.
Board escalation: The CEO brings the draft questions, and what is holding them up, to the Personnel Committee.
Why this point
The questions need confirming before the provider can build and test the survey.

Too few responses

When action is triggered
With two weeks of the survey left, fewer than half of whaiora have responded.
Agreed response
Management: Kaimahi encourage more whaiora to take part, and the CEO reports what was done.
Board escalation: The Board is told the final response rate and whether the results can be relied on.
Why this point
Two weeks leaves time to follow up with whaiora before the survey closes.
IVKPI Definition & ReportingWhat is measured, who is accountable, and how it is reported▾
Primary measureThe share of tāngata whaiora who submit the annual survey.
TargetTo decideAt least 50% taking part. No satisfaction or Net Promoter Score targets are set yet (see Section II).
TimeframeBy September 2026, then each year.
BaselineNone yet, because the survey has never been run. Sector benchmarks exist, and an independent provider would bring comparisons to help set targets.
KPI ownerThe CEO, named at the June 2026 workshop. The CEO is responsible for making the survey happen. The provider keeps it independent, so the results come to the Board unchanged.
Data sourceTo decideThe independent provider's report (provider not yet appointed).
Reporting scheduleTo decideThe wording implies once a year, but does not say when results reach the Board. Proposed: the provider's report goes to the first Board hui after the survey closes.
Review dateTo decideNot set yet. Proposed: the Board reviews the wording once the first results are in. If the Board uses the first survey as its agreed baseline, that is also when it would set the satisfaction targets.
Change protocolTo decideNot yet agreed. Proposed: the Change Protocol in the KPI Policy, with changes decided by the full Board on the Personnel Committee's recommendation where that is useful. See Section VI.
Outstanding mattersTo decideThe survey provider, the survey questions, the decision on outcome targets, the reporting schedule and the three action thresholds (see Section II).
Things to noteAs worded, the KPI measures taking part. It becomes a measure of outcomes once the Board sets satisfaction and Net Promoter Score targets.
VEvidence MapThe actions that lead to the result, and what proves each one▾
ActionWhat proves itWhere it comes from
Set up the surveyA provider appointed, and questions agreed for the six areas.Independent provider (not yet appointed)
Reach whaioraThe response rate each month while the survey is open, compared with the 50% target.Provider, or the CEO while the survey is open

VIChanging this KPIHow the Change Protocol in the KPI Policy applies to this KPI▾

This KPI follows the Change Protocol in the KPI Policy. Major changes require Board approval, while changes to monitoring may be approved under the CEO's delegated authority. The notes below are specific to KPI 6C.

  • Who may propose a change. The CEO, the Board, or a Board Committee (the Personnel Committee or the Audit, Finance and Risk Committee).
  • Proposing a major change. Any proposed major change must be put to the Board in writing, explaining:
    • What specifically is proposed to change?
    • Why is the change necessary?
    • How will it affect the target, measurement, or comparison with previous results?
    • Who has been consulted, and what decision is requested?
  • Who approves. The Board approves major changes, ordinarily on a recommendation from the Personnel Committee. This is the Board's first Kaupapa KPI, so any change goes to the full Board, on the Personnel Committee's recommendation where that is useful. Changes to leading indicators or action thresholds may be approved by the CEO where authorised, unless they are significant.
  • Where it is recorded. Minuted at the meeting, with the change proposal linked as reference material, and a new entry added to the KPI Record's Decision History.
  • What to expect. Leading indicators and action thresholds may be refined over time as the Board and management learn which measures provide the most useful early warning. Changes are approved according to the Change Protocol.
  • A decision already waiting. Whether to set outcome targets now or after the first survey (see Section II). Either choice changes the KPI's wording, so it goes through the Change Protocol.
  • Already required, not a change. Appointing the provider and agreeing the questions are already required by this KPI. They need an owner and a date. They do not need a change proposal.

Each entry is tagged, so trustees can tell what the Board approved from what was only proposed, reviewed or reported. The Board adds an entry each time it revisits the KPI.
